The evidence consistently shows that, for the U.S. federal government, the President has the power to approve or veto legislation, and Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote [d1, d5, d7, d8]. Document d9 complements this by showing a parallel structure at the state level for Virginia. Since all documents agree on the core concept and add different valid perspectives (federal process, state example, procedural details), they can be combined into a coherent answer.

The President of the United States has the constitutional power to approve or veto legislation passed by Congress [d1, d4, d7]. If the President vetoes a bill, Congress can override that veto with a two-thirds majority vote in both the House and Senate [d5, d7, d8]. This federal process is detailed in Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution [d6, d7]. At the state level, for example in Virginia, the Governor holds a similar veto power over bills passed by the state legislature [d9].
